The premium-due & pending journeys, mapped

Day 45 writes. Day 60 telephones. Nothing lapses quietly.

Both journeys, photographed from the engine running its own invented demo book — no real client appears anywhere on this page. Premium dues with Saira Ramnarine ($538.90 monthly, her bankers order stopped in May) and pending business with Javed Latchan (a $1M Flexiterm application waiting on one document). The chips show who acts at each step:

AUTOMATIC — the engine AGENT — the calls YOU — the manager moments CLIENT — their part
Part One

The premium-due journey

Saira Ramnarine · policy 9004100017 · $538.90 monthly · $1,616.70 outstanding · agent Tricia Baksh, unit manager Gary Sookdeo
45
First word
Day 45 — and not a day before

The engine writes first AUTOMATIC

Forty-four days of silence is deliberate: a premium a few days late is a banking timing difference, not a conversation. At day 45 the letter goes — warm, specific, her actual figures, six one-tap choices and a way to pay. Her agent, unit manager and branch manager are copied on the same email, so nobody finds out about the case later.

Her inbox — Tricia, Gary & you copied · scroll to read
  • A case-tracking code, not a phone number — replies route to branch support and are logged; the letter never exposes anyone’s cell
  • Contract wording is never paraphrased — the letter quotes the policy note verbatim or says nothing
  • The send is logged by policy and stage — the engine can be run twice, ten times, and this letter still goes once
  • Her answer (“fix my bankers order”, “review my premium”…) lands on the case for everyone to see
50
Every 5 days
Days 50 · 55 — the reminder rhythm, until day 60

Reminders count down; the agent works the book AGENT

Every five days a short reminder lands — each one counting down to the day-90 line. The moment Saira answers the reminders stop: the sequence is response-aware, so nobody who replied gets nagged. Meanwhile Tricia signs into the engine and sees her whole book, sorted by what lapses first — with Saira flagged and the week’s save spelled out.

↕ Tricia’s signed-in book — Saira flagged, priorities written for her
The day-50 reminder — “40 days remaining”
  • The survey answers from the 45-day letter route hardship cases to retention before day 60
  • Sorting is urgency, not raw days — a day-89 final outranks a nine-month-old file every time
60
It goes human
Day 60 — the one milestone the client doesn’t get as a letter

Handover: the manager telephones YOU

Day 60 is deliberately not another letter — it is where the case is handed to the manager, carrying the whole history: every letter sent, every answer given. The manager is asked to telephone and to confirm within 3 days — and because the advisor, the branch manager and the client are all copied, the commitment is public. One reply acknowledges it; then the 7-day feedback clock runs until there’s an outcome.

The day-60 handover — to the manager, everyone copied
The manager’s one-line reply, acknowledged
3 days
To confirm the case is in hand — chased every 3 days, all copied, until acknowledged
7 days
Once committed, feedback is awaited weekly until the case resolves
Private stays private
Manager-only questions never appear in any email the client is copied on
75
Then day 88
Days 75 · 88 — the last two letters

A personal note, then the final notice AUTOMATIC

Day 75 is a personal note in the unit manager’s name — Gary writing about Saira’s own policy, not a template shouting. Day 88 is the final notice, and it always sends, answered or not: someone who replied at day 46 and still owes at day 88 needs it more than anybody. It lands before the day-90 cliff — never on it.

Day 75 — from Gary Sookdeo, personally
Day 88 — the final notice, 2 days remaining
90
Endings
Day 90 and after — every file gets an ending in words

Paid, closing, or win-back — never silence CLIENT

Whichever way it goes, the file closes out loud. The moment the sheet shows her premium paying again, a thank-you letter goes and the case is done. If day 90 arrives unpaid, the closing question goes instead — “how did we do?” at days 90, 95 and 100, three rounds and then quiet, because the answer teaches the branch more than another demand would. From day 110 to 180 the win-back window is open: the policy can still be restored, and the letter says exactly how.

The good ending — account up to date
The closing question — days 90 · 95 · 100
45 — first letter→ 50 · 55 — reminders→ 60 — manager telephones→ 75 — personal note→ 88 — final notice→ 90–100 — closing→ 110–180 — win-back
Part Two

The pending journey

Javed Latchan · application 1000892336 · Flexiterm Convertible, $1M face · received 14 July · waiting on a Proof of Address — a completely separate clock from the dues ladder; the two flows never touch the same policy.
0
Seen
The morning the application appears in the sheet

Support sees it the day it lands AUTOMATIC

Every pending application joins the branch work queue the morning it appears — sorted by what unblocks it fastest, not by age alone: replacement gates first, settle-ready papers, our own entry errors, first premiums, then documents oldest-first. This is Sasha’s desk:

↕ The pendings desk — GATE → SETTLE → FIX → COLLECT → CHASE
  • The replacement gate — a new application from a client whose cover is lapsing gets flagged per the Sept 2022 guidelines: signed Declaration Form + ID with the application, or it’s Not Proceeded With
  • The ES400 grid is decoded — PCRC/PERC means underwriting is COMPLETE, so the case is settle-ready and jumps the queue
  • Suspense money is shown on the case — premium already paid and sitting idle is the strongest reason to move
21
Named
Day 21 of the application

The letter that names the document AUTOMATIC

Three weeks is enough grace for papers to arrive on their own. Then the letter goes — and it names the thing: “Proof of Address, outstanding 30 days,” not “outstanding requirements.” It shows where the application stands — received, today, and what happens on receipt — and if the missing item is the first premium, the payment button is right in the letter.

Javed’s inbox — agent & managers copied
35
Fortnights
Every 14 days until day 120 — then letters stop

The fortnightly ask — and the settle-ready flag AGENT

The same letter returns each fortnight, refreshed with what’s still outstanding — each round deduped, so a missed morning can’t double-send. Between letters the queue is the human push: the agent collects the paper in person. And the day underwriting completes, the letter changes its own tone — one document now stands between Javed and a policy in force.

The settle-ready variant — underwriting COMPLETE
  • Rounds land at day 21, 35, 49… with a 3-day window, so a run that misses a day still catches it
  • At day 120 the letters stop — a case that old is a management decision, not a mail-merge
  • If it closes any other way, the chase record stays — who was asked for what, and when
✓
In force
The morning the sheet shows it settled

The close, in front of everyone AUTOMATIC

The engine notices a pend-chased application turn into a policy in force and sends the note everyone was waiting for: received 14 July, completed in 48 days, Flexiterm Convertible, in force — with MyGG as the next step. It fires exactly once, and the client, the agent and the managers are on the same letter, so the good news closes the loop for everyone it involved.

“Your policy is in force” — everyone on one letter
Part Three

The group lane

Schemes like Servus and the bankers’ pensions are companies, not chase lists — their members never receive an arrears letter.
14
Rhythm
One statement per scheme, per fortnight — opens at day 45

One statement per scheme AUTOMATIC

Member policies are gathered under the company. The scheme administrator — or, if none is configured, the servicing agent, never the email on a member’s record — gets one remittance statement: which month’s remittance looks missed, who is closest to the day-90 cliff, and how many ancient positions are counted without being paraded. Three asks, one page.

The Servus statement — to the administrator, agents copied

Ready when you are — the pilot in 3 steps

Paste the one file into Apps Script.

From GitHub → your script project: PremiumDue-ALL-IN-ONE.gs. Set the fresh staff key in Script Properties — the key lives in the editor, never in code, never on GitHub.

Stats before letters.

Run pdPilotStats first — the branch digest below lands in your inbox and nothing else moves. Read it, check the counts against what you know, and only then let letters render.

Pilot on yourself and Neil.

Set TEST_INBOX to your own email and PILOT_AGENTS to you and Neil Ramnanan, then run dailyPremiumDueRun. Every letter re-routes to your inbox with a [TEST] banner naming who would have received it and who would have been copied. When it reads right: DRY_RUN false · TEST_INBOX empty · GO_LIVE_CONFIRM true — three keys, in that order, and the first live run starts on a clean slate.

The pilot’s first email — the branch digest, before any letter
Still needed from you before the real send: the fresh staff key (in the runbook — never committed) · your and Neil’s agent names exactly as the sheet spells them · the scheme administrator addresses for the group lane.
Every screen on this page was produced by running the engine’s committed code on its invented demo book — 9004-1000xx policies, 555 phone numbers, example.com addresses. Nothing was sent to anyone, and no real client, policy or contact appears. The cadence shown — 45 / every-5-days / 60 / 75 / 88 / 90–100 / 110–180, pendings 21 then fortnightly to 120, groups fortnightly from day 45 — is the cadence pinned by the engine’s test suites.
